claims.text: Group IV-containing refractory high-entropy alloys are susceptible to oxygen-related secondary-phase formation and embrittlement.
Hydride decomposition leaves a highly reactive metal powder that is especially prone to oxygen uptake.
Rapid, multi-stage hydride decomposition minimizes oxygen exposure and prevents brittle alpha-HCP and oxide formation.
Hydride decomposition and extrusion require ultra-high vacuum or inert gas with oxygen partial pressure below 10^-8 Pa.
A sealed, oxygen-scavenged, Ti-gettered container prevents oxygen uptake during hydride decomposition.
Hf/Ti hydrides should be heated at 50–100 °C/min to 400–500 °C, just above their decomposition onset.
Immediate high-pressure extrusion at 1000–1100 °C provides plasticity while avoiding grain growth.
High-pressure extrusion refines the grains and increases dislocation density.
Cooling faster than 100 °C/min suppresses nucleation of equilibrium brittle phases.
Aging at 600–700 °C after rapid cooling can generate coherent nanoscale precipitates.
The desired coherent precipitates can be B2 or Laves-type while the alloy retains a BCC matrix.
Coherent nanoscale precipitation strengthens the alloy through order hardening and lattice-misfit effects without premature cracking.
The proposed process will produce a bulk alloy exceeding 99% of theoretical density.
The proposed process will limit oxygen content to below 0.1 wt%.
The processed alloy will have a single-phase BCC or metastable solid-solution structure.
The processed alloy will have yield strength above 1.0 GPa at 800 °C.
The processed alloy will retain more than 10% room-temperature ductility.
Slow heating or open-atmosphere processing produces material with more than 0.5 wt% oxygen.
Slow heating or open-atmosphere processing produces cracking, alpha-HCP and oxide precipitates, and low yield strength.
The oxide-nucleation threshold for Hf/Ti at 1000 °C is approximately 10^-6 Pa oxygen partial pressure.

contradictions.description: The mediator and mechanism require distinct B2 or Laves-type precipitates, whereas the predicted outcome describes the product as single-phase BCC or a single metastable solid solution. A precipitate-strengthened microstructure is not single-phase unless the intended B2 ordering is being treated only as local order, which is not stated and does not resolve the Laves-phase example.
